cf.title: Allow subquery pull-up past inlineable CTEs

input.subject: [PATCH] Allow subquery pull-up past inlineable CTEs

verdict_reasoning: Only demand-1 survived, and it is fixable. The thread shows no real-world query, but the extra planning work falls only on subqueries that were rejected before, and the existing code marks this gap with an XXX comment. So no level fails. What remains is a planner committer's judgment on plan changes and on the cases the patch prose leaves open, such as recursive CTEs.

brief.title: Allow subquery pull-up when all its CTEs are inlineable
brief.problem: is_simple_subquery() rejects any subquery with a non-empty cteList, even after SS_process_ctes has inlined every CTE. The subquery is then planned separately, so the outer query cannot use join conditions inside it, for example a parameterized index scan through an outer join. This affects queries that put an inlineable WITH inside a subquery.
brief.proposed_design: The patch moves the CTE inlining checks from SS_process_ctes() into is_cte_inlineable(). is_simple_subquery() accepts a subquery whose CTEs all pass that check, and rejects one with any unreferenced SELECT CTE. pull_up_simple_subquery() inlines the CTEs on its copy of the subquery and clears cteList, so the original RTE stays intact if pull-up is abandoned.
author_claims: A tenk1/tenk2 example changes from a hash join with a full seq scan to a nested loop with 10 index lookups.
Extra planning cost hits only subqueries that were rejected before, so the pull-up gain pays for it.
MATERIALIZED, volatile, multiply-referenced and unreferenced CTEs still block pull-up.
An existing with.sql plan loses a Subquery Scan, which the author calls the expected improvement.
brief.thread_state: Only reviewer Xinlei (Clemenza) Zhang replied; she tested v2, found results identical to the equivalent no-CTE query, and reported no new issues. No committer has commented, and the CommitFest entry is in Needs review.
unclear: The first example's before-plan did not reproduce on master; the thread does not say whether that example was replaced in the tests.
The patch prose does not say how recursive CTEs, data-modifying CTEs, or CTEs referenced from nested sublevels are handled.
There are no planning-time measurements for queries with many or large CTEs.
The patch prose does not say whether plans of existing user queries can change for the worse after pull-up.

objections.title: No real-world query shown that needs a WITH inside a pulled-up subquery
objections.failure_scenario: A committer takes on new prepjointree.c logic, kept in step with SS_process_ctes() through is_cte_inlineable(), for a case shown only on regression tables. If few users write WITH inside a subquery, the project pays for that coupling and gets little back.
objections.argument: Every example in messages #1 and #3 is synthetic, and message #2 found that the first one did not reproduce. No field report, -general or -bugs thread, or production workload appears in the material. Hand-written queries can move the WITH to the top level, where it is already inlined. [P8] was declined on the same ground, though there the cost fell on everyone and here it mostly does not.
objections.author_must_show: Which real queries, for example views defined with WITH or ORM-generated SQL used under outer joins, hit this today, and why can their authors not move the WITH to the top level?

precedents.title: Pull up sublink of type 'NOT NOT (expr)'

critic.reasoning: The thread shows only regression-table examples and no user report, and a view defined with WITH is a plausible case but is not shown. [P8] must not be used as support, because there the cost fell on every query.

refuted.title: Pull-up gate relies on SS_process_ctes behavior that it does not share
refuted.failure_scenario: A later patch changes how SS_process_ctes treats some kind of CTE, such as unreferenced CTEs or a new materialization option, but leaves SS_all_ctes_inlineable() and SS_inline_ctes() unchanged. The subquery is then pulled up and its cteList cleared, so that CTE is dropped or handled differently than at its own level. No regression test fails unless that exact case has a test.
refuted.argument: After this patch, CTE inlining happens in two phases: SS_process_ctes at the query's own level and SS_inline_ctes inside pull_up_simple_subquery. is_cte_inlineable() is shared, but the cterefcount == 0 rule copies knowledge that SS_process_ctes skips such CTEs (message #3), and that knowledge is not shared code. The thread found this kind of drift once already, in the comment on SS_all_ctes_inlineable() (message #2). A committer would likely want one routine that both paths call, or an assertion that fails loudly when they disagree.
refuted.author_must_show: Can SS_process_ctes and the pull-up path share one routine that both inlines and keeps CTEs, so that a later change to CTE handling cannot reach only one of them?

critic.reasoning: The patch already puts the inlining decision in is_cte_inlineable(), which both paths call, so a new materialization option reaches both. The separate cterefcount == 0 rule only blocks pull-up, so a later change there cannot drop a CTE.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: subselect.h gains new exported helpers (SS_all_ctes_inlineable, SS_inline_ctes); no existing signature changes.

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: Subqueries with inlineable CTEs are now pulled up, so plans of existing queries can change.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: CTE inlining now also runs inside pull_up_simple_subquery, a second call site next to SS_process_ctes.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: is_simple_subquery now walks each CTE query tree for subqueries that have a WITH; no planning-time numbers are shown.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which real queries, such as views defined with WITH or ORM-generated SQL under outer joins, hit this restriction today?
How does the pull-up path handle recursive CTEs and CTEs referenced from a nested sublevel of the subquery?
What is the planning-time cost for a subquery with many or large CTEs, including the case where pull-up is abandoned at the recheck?
Have you found any existing query whose plan gets worse after the subquery is pulled up?
Do the with.sql tests now use the tenk1/tenk2 example from message #3 in place of the one that did not reproduce on master?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows planner preprocessing: subquery pull-up in prepjointree.c and CTE handling in subselect.c. No committer has spoken in the visible thread.
committability.liability: Plan changes and any wrong-result bug for queries with a WITH inside a pulled-up subquery, plus keeping the two inlining call sites in step, for as long as the code exists.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v2 one day after the review and said he will continue from another email address; the entry is tagged My First Patch.

priority.reason: The patch is about 14 KiB, adds no user-visible surface and removes a restriction the code already marks with an XXX comment. The thread shows only regression-table examples, so the audience is not known, and planner pull-up code needs a careful read.

provisional_note: Without the code, the handling of recursive CTEs, CTEs referenced from nested sublevels, and permission info of inlined CTEs could not be checked. Only 3 of 6 thread messages were visible.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Consider parallel for LATERAL subqueries having LIMIT/OFFSET
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes set_rel_consider_parallel so that a lateral subquery with LIMIT/OFFSET may still be considered for parallel query, so a Gather can go above the whole nested loop. A later version allows this only when rel->lateral_relids is not empty.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author argued that each outer row gets its own execution of the limited subquery, but Tom Lane (seen only in quoted text) and Robert Haas were not convinced this is safe. Tom Lane noted that the patch took any lateral dependency as enough, even one that does not feed the limited subquery. Robert Haas said the real issue is where parameters are set and used, which the LATERAL keyword does not capture. The commitfest manager returned it because no further review was coming, and asked for a more rigorous correctness argument or simpler constraints.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The problem here isn't created by LATERAL, but by parameters.

precedents_retrieved.title: Parallelize correlated subqueries that execute within each worker
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner build parallel plans for queries with correlated subplans when each subplan runs entirely within one parallel worker, so no Param value has to pass between workers. After review, the design changed to treat PARAM_EXEC params as parallel safe by default, track required params on each rel, and insert a Gather node only where that set is empty.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread shows no author reply after Tomas Vondra's July 2024 review, and the entry was returned with feedback in October 2024. That review found that regression tests failed on a changed plan in select_parallel, reported a compiler warning, and listed code comments. It also said no reviewer was able to confirm that the PARAM handling is correct.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: And in general the patch looks reasonably simple and clean, but my knowledge of PARAM intricacies is pretty much nil, so I'm hesitant to claim the patch is correct.

precedents_retrieved.title: allow partial union-all and improve parallel subquery costing
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner build partial paths for UNION ALL so the branches can run under a parallel plan. It also changes subquery costing to account for parallelism, with a regression test and before/after plans for TPC-DS query 5.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No reviewer took up the patch during the commitfests. In March 2021 the patch no longer applied, and the entry was set to Waiting for Author. The author sent no rebased patch, so the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Since no new patch has been provided, marking this Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: add explicit partial union-all and improve parallel subquery costing
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner build partial Append paths for UNION ALL subqueries so their branches can run in parallel. It also changes subquery scan costing to take parallel workers into account in the row estimate.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author stopped responding after Ronan Dunklau's review asked for a regression test of the new partial append path and questioned the subquery scan row estimate change. Daniel Gustafsson closed the entry because the thread stalled with these requests unanswered. An earlier round was also closed after the patch needed a rebase and no new version came in time.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
With the thread stalled and requests for a test (documentation really?) not
responded to I'm marking this patch Returned with Feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Pulling up direct-correlated ANY_SUBLINK
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets the planner pull up an ANY sublink whose subquery references the immediate outer query level (varlevelsup = 1) by rewriting it as an EXISTS sublink. Today convert_ANY_sublink_to_join gives up on such sublinks, so they run as SubPlans.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane found the patch messy because it duplicated code from elsewhere, and he posted a different approach that drops the contain_vars_of_level restriction and uses LATERAL. Richard Guo showed that without a limit on outer references, LATERAL constraints can leave no legal join order ("failed to build any 3-way joins"). The v2 patch then stopped applying on HEAD, nobody posted a rebased version, and the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This patch seems awfully messy to me.  The fact that you're having to
duplicate stuff done elsewhere suggests at the least that you've not
plugged the code into the best place.

This reverts 66c0185a3 (Allow planner to use Merge Append to

precedents_retrieved.title: Pull up sublink of type 'NOT NOT (expr)'
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes any number of consecutive NOTs over a SubLink in pull_up_sublinks, so that quals like "NOT NOT (a.i in (select ...))" or "NOT NOT EXISTS (...)" can be pulled up into joins. Today such SubLinks stay as SubPlans.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane argued that pull_up_sublinks runs before transformations that could create NOT NOT, so it only sees NOT NOT that a user wrote by hand, and no one showed that this happens in real queries. Without such evidence the extra code and planning cycles would be a net loss for everyone else. Running expression simplification before pullup would need a second simplification pass, which he judged not worth the cost. The author agreed and asked for the patch to be rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So I'm inclined to reject this patch as probably being a net loss in
almost all cases.  If you can show any real-world cases where it wins,
we could reconsider.

precedents_retrieved.title: Make transformAExprIn() return a flattened bool expression directly
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes transformAExprIn() emit one flat OR (or AND) list for an IN expression with non-constant elements, so it no longer emits nested binary bool expressions. The stated aim is to save planner work by doing the flattening in the parser.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the parser should not perform optimizations. He added that this change assumes all parse- and rewrite-time code handles non-binary AND and OR nodes, and that it may change view dump output. No evidence of a measurable gain was offered, and an earlier test showed the same plan before and after the patch because the planner already flattens these nodes. The entry was withdrawn after that message.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
In general, it is not the business of the parser to perform
optimizations.  Where we have done that, we've often regretted it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use simplehash.h instead of dynahash in SMgr
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the dynahash table that smgr.c uses to look up SMgrRelation entries with a simplehash table, using a small entry that points to the SMgrRelationData, plus a custom hash function; it made recovery about 10% faster in the author's benchmark. Because simplehash does not keep pointers to entries stable, the author later replaced this with a new hash table implementation (generichash) that uses segments and bitmaps.
precedents_retrieved.objection: After the change to a new hash table implementation, Thomas Munro questioned adding another hash table and making the hash table provide fast iteration over its items. The author reports that Andres Freund also opposed the design, saying bitmaps are slow, but those messages are off-list and not shown. With no consensus and no update for two months, the patch no longer applied, and Michael Paquier marked it returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Thomas made it quite clear it's not for the patch, and on discussing the patch with Andres, it turned out he does not like the idea either.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent matches this idea. [P8]'s demand concern applies only weakly, because views defined with WITH produce this shape and only such subqueries pay the planning cost. [P5] died over duplicated code, while this patch moves the inlining checks into one helper. The thread cites no earlier discussion beyond the existing XXX comment quoted in message #1.

The patch changes no syntax, GUC, catalog, dump format or psql output. Plans can change for existing queries that put a default or NOT MATERIALIZED CTE inside a subquery, but that matches what the docs already promise for inlineable CTEs, and MATERIALIZED and OFFSET 0 still work as optimization fences. Data-modifying CTEs are already rejected below the top level, and the patch prose does not say how recursive CTEs are handled, which only the code can show.

The proposal changes only planner behaviour in subselect.c and prepjointree.c. It adds no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog column, catversion bump or protocol message, and stored view definitions keep their form. The new subselect.h helpers add symbols and change no existing struct or signature, so extensions are not affected.

The patch only changes planner join-tree flattening for queries the user already has permission to run, and it adds no privilege, role, GUC or catalog surface. Subqueries marked security_barrier and RLS security quals keep their existing pull-up limits, and permission checks move up with the pulled-up range table as they do for other pull-ups. Whether the inlined CTEs' permission info merges correctly can only be checked in the code.

From this angle the patch is small and general. It removes a long-standing XXX restriction, and the extra planning work runs only for subqueries that were rejected before. No committer has engaged yet, and the author is new to the project, so ownership after commit is open. That is a committability issue, not an objection to the idea.

Postgres has no existing feature, extension or hook that removes this subquery boundary. The only workaround is a manual query rewrite, either moving the WITH to the top level or dropping it, and that is not a feature. The patch reuses the existing inlining checks through a shared is_cte_inlineable() and does not add a second mechanism. The existing code also marks the gap with an XXX comment.
Only a show-demand objection applies. The extra planning cost falls only on subqueries that were rejected before, so who-pays-versus-who-gains does not fail here.
